newsitem.title: USA: AT&T, SBC merger talk draws fire.
newsitem.headline: AT&T, SBC merger talk draws fire.

text.p: Reports on Tuesday that AT&T Corp was in merger talks with regional Baby Bell SBC Communications Inc drew sharp criticism from telecommunications and antitrust experts.
Such a deal would raise problems for competition authorities, foreign competitors and consumers, the experts said.
"We've come full circle," said Jeffrey Olson of the law firm of Paul, Weiss in Washington, who worked on the 1980s legal decision that split the Baby Bells from AT&T.
"One of the only substantive restrictions imposed on AT&T at the time of the divestiture under the consent decree was that it couldn't acquire any of the Bell Operating Companies."

That has changed. A telecommunications law passed last year was aimed in part at permitting local and long distance companies to compete in each other's markets. As a result, some of the local operating companies have already merged.
The Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday that AT&T was in merger talks with SBC, which provides local phone service in seven states, including California.

James Love, of consumer advocacy group Center for Study of Responsive Law, said that if the merger takes place there will be fewer heavyweight companies to fight with local companies before state utility regulators.
"It makes a big difference if a company like AT&T or MCI weighs in," he said. "The regulators listen to the big guys." By contrast, he said, consumers have a far weaker voice before state regulators.
Foreign phone companies might also be jarred.
Such a merger "would drive (Japan's) Nippon Telegraph and Telephone crazy," Olson said.

"They've spent the last five years being threatened with divestiture ... they've got to look at this and say, 'My God, what are you doing to us?' I think they would run off to their own regulators and say, 'stop the presses'," he said.
Others noted that it will be tough to get the deal past U.S. regulators.

While it is "entirely possible" that the two firms have held talks, "we ascribe a low probability of ultimate approval because of the implications for competition," said Merrill Lynch analyst Dan Reingold.
Steve Axinn, of the antitrust firm of Axinn, Veltrop & Harkrider in New York, said the merger faced a rocky road.

"The kneejerk instinct of the Justice Department is going to be to attack," he said. But the final resolution, he added, will depend on "what the parties are able to provide in terms of factual support for their position."
